Reuse and buy an existing house, you'll get more for your money and the environmental damage has already been done. Plus, you won't have sunk $60~$200k into something that has ZERO VALUE to anyone else, essentially having lit that money on fire.

RV, you can get an Awesome used bus for under $10k. Tiny-houses are NOT "nomadic", they are the worst of RV's and houses with none of the benefits. Some people are laughing all the way to the bank and proving once again that fools are easily parted with their money.
Really? They look great in the the pictures but now that you bring it up, I can see you're right.

They are a creation of media, probably born out of 100% off-grid cabins ~ but even those are placed legally. Except they have been targeted towards the urban crowd, who want to keep living in urban environments.. but you can't just park one of those on the street. You can't put it on a vacant lot either (city codes will prevent that), and Most cities don't allow long-term "parking" of these things on residential lots either (adds extra strain to a sewer system that wasn't designed to handle the additional load). So that leaves commercial, AKA trailer and RV parks. If you're going to live in one of those, why not simply buy (for less money) a trailer or RV?

It's just not practical. They are sold on the Dream/Idea, not the real world practicality. If you know of anyone Seriously interested, slap some sense into them. You can get one hell of a nice RV (for which you can get a HOME LOAN) for $20k ~https://phoenix.craigslist.org/cph/rvs/5968391406.html ~ or cheaper if you want to DIY some (yellow school buses are frequently sold for in the $5~6k range). Good for a single or couple, with kids gets harder but isn't impossible.... of course, RV/Trailer park monthly rent is often the same or more expensive than a mortgage (Austin, TX for $525/month ~ http://austinrvpark.com/)).
Can you really get a good RV for $20K? I'll check your Craig's List link. I would love to have a reliable RV -- I do public speaking and I tour a lot.

There's 2 different definitions of "good". The first is being good enough to live in full time, that's all about layout and not leaking. Both are pretty easy to obtain. The second is using it for lots of driving, that's adding a bit more. Personal opinion, but bus conversions seem to have the edge here as they're Designed for lots of highway use where dedicated RV's leave a lot of be desired. If you're going to invest in something like that do 2 things, be Brutally honest about how you would use the RV, including how much. If not much, then renting is always better. Me, I have a van because I only wanted a more water-resistant roof over my head (I stepped up from tent camping) while also needing to retain the functionality of a truck that I had to sell so I had room for the van. I'll probably never go more than a month in a row living out of the van, don't need water tanks, a bathroom, shower, oven, etc... cost, complexity, things to go wrong. I still cook nearly all of my own meals though, so a cook-top (induction that can run from shore power OR my solar/battery system) and fridge (again electric, tied into my solar system) were still necessary. That may not work before for your ideal needs, but just pointing out things you need to be honest with yourself about.

The second thing? Find a GOOD independent mechanic who can do a pre-purchase inspection of anything you're considering buying (or for follow-up work). One of my career arks was as a motorcycle mechanic and I still fix and flip bikes (plus do the occasional inspection/repair work), a vehicle can look great on the surface and have thousand of dollars worth of headache just below that will stop you from enjoying the vehicle. I've seen it absolutely kill budgets and any desire to use the vehicle. I've seen a number of less-than-pretty but mechanically flawless bikes that were sold stupid cheap to people who thoroughly enjoyed them too. Point is, get it inspected before purchasing. But yes, with time you can Really find a good RV for $20~30k, sometimes less and always more. If you do start looking, shear common snow-bird destinations as those markets seem to have the largest selection and fly-n-drive experiences are a LOT of fun.

Thanks for the info -- I'll make sure I get an indie mechanic to inspect before buying. I have a good guy. One of my dilemmas though is Class C or 5th wheel. The class C is really comfortable for travel but I've heard they don't last long before having problems, and they're hard to park, and they're hard to get around in when you're kin a city. A 5th wheel, you can detach the truck and you have local transportation. But you have to find a place to park it which means pay for RV campground, or something.

That's why I went for the Sprinter Van. It fits in a normal parking spot, isn't worse to drive around than a full sized truck, and holds everything I need. Plus, I can "stealth camp", park in a parking lot and it's not weird to see a work van. Try the same with a 5th wheel or RV and it doesn't work as well. Granted, my path is Not for everyone. Apparently you can still "stealth camp" with a big RV, it's just pulling into a residential area after dark and leaving before sun-up.... neighbors who would normally complain will most likely just think you're visiting someone or so-and-so just bought a new RV (apparently this works best with very nice looking RVs).

If you Need further transportation after arriving, the RV with toad (towed vehicle) works as well as a 5th wheel plus you don't have to drive around in a monster truck on narrow city streets.

Whatever path you decide, all the best...
